title: Identity, authorization and audit
summary: Follow one request from the principal that authenticates, through whose permissions apply and what filters and masks return, to the audit rows that prove what happened, and finish with a narrow, tested access review.
objectives: Tell users, service principals and groups apart, and SCIM provisioning from identity and token federation.
Choose OAuth U2M, OAuth M2M, workload identity federation or a secret scope for a caller, and avoid the token exposure mistakes each prevents.
Predict the acting principal, the failure layer and the rows and values returned under row filters, column masks and attribute-based policies.
Write a least-privilege plan with a must-fail test matrix, separated duties and an audit-based incident sequence.

sections.title: What you will be able to do
How a caller proves who it is
Secrets stay in a scope, not in code
Whose permissions apply, and where it fails
Row filters, column masks and attribute-based policies
Audit rows as evidence after a leak
Your turn: a dashboard and an export

questions.prompt: A job that authenticates as sp-nightly-ingest with OAuth M2M fails with PERMISSION_DENIED naming USE SCHEMA on schema quality.raw. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The OAuth secret expired, so it must be rotated.
options.rationale: An expired secret fails at the token request, before any schema is named.

options.text: The credential worked; Unity Catalog refused because the service principal lacks USE SCHEMA on quality.raw.
options.rationale: An authentication failure would name no object; a refusal that names a privilege and a schema comes after authentication succeeded.

options.text: The row filter on the raw table excluded every row.
options.rationale: Filters return fewer rows without an error; they never produce PERMISSION_DENIED.

options.text: The job should run as its creator, whose grants include USE SCHEMA.
options.rationale: Moving production work back to a person widens access and hides who acted; grant USE SCHEMA to the service principal's group instead.

questions.prompt: Which way of giving the nightly job the supplier SFTP password keeps it out of code, job output and Git while leaving one control over who can read it?

options.text: Write it as a literal in the notebook's first cell and ask reviewers not to open that cell.
options.rationale: The literal travels with every export, clone and commit of the notebook.

options.text: Pass it as a job parameter in the job's settings.
options.rationale: Parameters are part of the job definition and run details, readable by anyone who can view them.

options.text: Print it once in a test run to confirm it works, then delete the output.
options.rationale: Output can be copied before it is deleted, and redaction does not recognise transformed values; only the ACL controls reading.

options.text: Store it in scope supplier-sftp, grant READ to ingest-jobs, and read it at run time with dbutils.secrets.get.
options.rationale: The value never appears in code, and the scope's ACL is the single place that decides who may read it.

questions.prompt: sp-supplier-portal's SELECT on quality.shared.supplier_rejections fails with PERMISSION_DENIED naming USE SCHEMA on quality.shared. Which change is the least-privilege fix?

options.text: Grant SELECT on catalog quality to the supplier-portal group.
options.rationale: It widens reads to every table in the catalog and still lacks the USE SCHEMA the error names.

options.text: Add sp-supplier-portal to the admins group.
options.rationale: Administrator membership clears the error by granting everything, the broad fix a review forbids.

options.text: Grant USE SCHEMA on quality.shared to the supplier-portal group.
options.rationale: It supplies exactly the privilege the error names, to the group that holds the portal's other grants.

options.text: Make sp-supplier-portal the owner of schema quality.shared.
options.rationale: Ownership hands over full control of the schema, including granting to others, when one usage privilege was missing.

cards.prompt: Why should a production job not run as the engineer who built it?
cards.answer: It would act with the engineer's own grants, require a person to hold production write access, and record every change under that person's name.
cards.explanation: The SDK recommends service principals for production jobs so interactive users need no write, delete or modify privilege in production. A job running as a person also breaks when that person moves team or leaves, and its audit rows cannot be told apart from the person's own actions.

cards.prompt: What changes when an identity administrator moves a user from one group to another?
cards.answer: Her effective access follows the new membership after the next sync, while every grant stays exactly as it was written.
cards.explanation: Grants name groups, and members inherit them, including through nested groups. Removing Maya from plant-eu-analysts removes every grant that reached her through it without anyone editing a GRANT statement, which is why group membership is itself an access decision to review.

cards.prompt: What does SCIM provisioning do that token federation never does?
cards.answer: SCIM creates, updates and removes users, groups and memberships in the account; token federation only decides which issuer's tokens are accepted.
cards.explanation: SCIM is how identities come to exist and disappear, for example when HR disables a leaver in the identity provider. Token federation maps an incoming token to an identity that must already exist, typically synced by SCIM, and neither mechanism grants a privilege.

cards.prompt: After an OAuth U2M sign-in, what stays on the laptop, and why protect it?
cards.answer: Cached access and refresh tokens issued to the signed-in person; the refresh token can mint new access tokens without a browser prompt.
cards.explanation: The tool exchanged an authorization code and a PKCE verifier for these tokens, and every later call acts as that person. The token cache is therefore a credential: keep it off shared machines and containers, and revoke sessions when a device is lost.

cards.prompt: In OAuth M2M, what does a service principal send to the token endpoint, and what comes back?
cards.answer: Its client ID, which is its application ID, and an OAuth secret; it receives an access token with an expiry to send as a bearer header.
cards.explanation: This is the client-credentials grant. A wrong, expired or deleted secret fails right here, before any object is named, while a valid token without a grant fails later with PERMISSION_DENIED. The SDK refreshes the access token shortly before it expires.

cards.prompt: Which fields of a federation policy decide whether a CI token may act as a service principal?
cards.answer: The issuer, the subject naming the permitted workload, and the audience, which defaults to the Databricks account ID.
cards.explanation: Workload identity federation exchanges a token issued by the CI platform for a Databricks token for one service principal, with no Databricks secret stored anywhere. A token from another workflow context, such as a pull request, carries a different subject and is refused.

cards.prompt: Why does changing a password not contain a leaked personal access token?
cards.answer: The token is a separate bearer credential with its own lifetime, so it keeps working until it expires or is revoked.
cards.explanation: The API only checks that a presented token is valid and then acts as its owner. Containment is revocation by the owner or deletion by an administrator; deleting the commit or making the repository private does not remove copies that were already made.

cards.prompt: Why is redaction of secrets in notebook output not an access control?
cards.answer: A principal allowed to read a secret can still reveal it, for example by transforming or copying it; only the ACL decides who reads.
cards.explanation: Databricks makes an effort to redact secret values it recognises when they are displayed, and its SDK states that permitted users cannot be prevented from reading secrets. Design the scope's ACL narrowly and treat redaction as a convenience, not a boundary.

cards.prompt: Whose privileges does Unity Catalog check when someone clicks Run now on a job?
cards.answer: Those of the job's run-as identity, such as sp-nightly-ingest, not those of the person who triggered the run.
cards.explanation: Triggering is an action on the job; the reads and writes inside the run are performed as the run-as identity. Permission to trigger or edit such a job is therefore an indirect route to the service principal's grants, which an access review has to list.

cards.prompt: How do you tell a row filter problem from a missing SELECT privilege by the symptom alone?
cards.answer: A missing privilege raises PERMISSION_DENIED naming it; a filter returns a successful result with fewer or zero rows.
cards.explanation: Filters and masks never raise errors, so an empty success points at the filter function or the caller's group memberships, while an error naming a privilege points at grants. Checking grants for an empty result wastes time and invites a wrong fix such as a wider grant.

cards.prompt: What must match between a column mask function and the column it masks?
cards.answer: The function's first argument must take the column's type, and the function should return that same type.
cards.explanation: A mask replaces values while the column keeps its type, so queries and tools downstream see an unchanged schema. Further columns can be passed as extra arguments, letting a mask decide on another column's value as well as on the caller's identity.

cards.prompt: What does a tag-based mask policy on a schema do to an untagged sensitive column in a new table?
cards.answer: Nothing: the policy matches columns by tag, so the untagged column is returned exactly as stored.
cards.explanation: An attribute-based policy applies to its securable and every descendant, but only to columns its condition matches. The control moves to tagging discipline, which is why tag assignment has its own roles and why an untagged column belongs in the test matrix as a must-fail case.

cards.prompt: What can the audit log system table not tell you about a successful read?
cards.answer: What the reader did with the rows afterwards, and whether a person or someone holding a copied token made the request.
cards.explanation: Audit rows record the time, service and action, acting identity, request parameters, source address and response. They are evidence of API actions, so pair them with job change history and identity-provider sign-in logs, and note when each query ran because delivery can lag.

cards.prompt: What is the first action after finding a leaked token, and why must it precede the investigation?
cards.answer: Revoke the token, because every minute spent analysing is a minute in which the finder can still act as its owner.
cards.explanation: Revocation also closes the exposure window that bounds the evidence search. After it, fix the window, query audit rows inside it, list what the identity could reach, rotate every readable secret and remove the cause, recording the time of each step.

cards.prompt: Why does a least-privilege test matrix need must-fail rows as well as must-succeed rows?
cards.answer: A plan that is too wide still passes every must-succeed row; only the denials show that a grant is narrow.
cards.explanation: Granting SELECT on a whole catalog lets the portal read its table and every neighbour. For each allowed request add a sibling table, a write, a parent-level read, another principal, rows outside the filter and a masked column, and run them as the real principal.
